Unlike sibling methods that may perform shading in a separate post-processing stage or require complex normal quantization, congradient shading operates as a pipeline with the viewing process, accruing no additional time for shading because the congradient calculation time is much less than the projection time [S2, book].

The evidence explicitly states that unlike other voxel-based systems that perform shading in a separate post-processor, the congradient shading unit is an integral part of the projection process. It further confirms that 'no additional time is accrued for the shading' because the 'congradient calculation time for each pixel is much less than its projection time.' This directly supports every part of the claim.

# Main pipeline: interleaved projection and shading [S2, book]

The evidence explicitly states that the shading unit is an integral part of the projection process (S2 notes point 1, passage paragraph 2). It confirms that each projected pixel is pipelined through memory access, projection, and shading units (S2 notes point 2, passage paragraph 2). It details that the projection stage generates 'congradient values' holding concatenated color and local gradient (S2 notes point 3, passage paragraph 2). It specifies that the production time of a congradient value is interleaved with the projection time of the next pixel (S2 notes point 4, passage paragraph 2). It mentions the display stage uses standard hardware and look-up tables for shading based on light source parameters (S2 notes point 5 & 6, passage paragraph 2). It notes that light source location can be arbitrarily changed for motion parallax (S2 notes point 7, passage paragraph 1). It describes Unidirectional and Bidirectional shading approaches suitable for hardware (S2 notes point 8, passage paragraph 3). Finally, it states no additional time is accrued for shading because congradient calculation time is much less than projection time (S2 notes point 9, passage paragraph 2).

A technique to accelerate rendering by precomputing illumination for each possible encoded gradient direction index, storing results in a table independent of color [S4, book].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S4]. The source explicitly states that illumination is computed once for each possible encoded gradient index and stored in a table. It further clarifies that because data samples with the same encoded gradient may have different colors, the stored illumination value represents the portion of the shading equation independent of color. The source also mentions that this precomputed illumination is typically an array of values (for ambient, diffuse, and specular components), which aligns with the claim's description.
